newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rand, inflation depress SAfrica business confidence.
newsitem.headline: Rand, inflation depress SAfrica business confidence.

text.p: Business confidence in South Africa plumbed its lowest level in 14 months in October amid a weaker rand/dollar exchange rate, rising inflation and higher short-term interest rates, a business grouping said on Tuesday.

The South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said its Business Confidence Index (BCI) -- a barometer which tracks the business mood in the country -- last month fell by 1.6 percentage points to 114.3, its lowest level since August 1995.
Despite this fall Sacob was still confident that South Africa would achieve GDP growth of around three percent, said Ben van Rensburg, director of economic policy.
"The lower BCI (shows)...the business cycle has taken a turn and is moving in a downward direction...but we still expect a growth rate of plus-minus three percent," van Rensburg told reporters.
Factors which depressed confidence in October included the exchange rate of the rand against the U.S. dollar which weakened to an average 4.70 in October compared to 4.54 in late September.

Further negative influences were a 0.9 percentage point increase in consumer inflation to 8.4 percent, and higher short-term trading rates, represented by the rate on three-month Bankers' Acceptances.
A lower dollar gold price, a decline in merchandise imports and the higher cost of building plans passed in October also took their toll on confidence, Sacob said.
But a number of positive factors were also present during October, it said.
These included an increase in real retail sales, a rise in merchandise export volumes and a surge in new passenger vehicle sales.

South African new car sales rose 28.4 percent to 27,816 units in October -- the highest monthly sales since June 1982, figures released by the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa showed on Tuesday.
Other factors propping up confidence were a reduction in the number of insolvencies and an increase in the average price of shares traded on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in October, Sacob said.
